local_facts.title: North Carolina puts the estimate in writing by statute
local_facts.claim: G.S. 20-354.3 of the North Carolina Motor Vehicle Repair Act requires a motor vehicle repair business, when a customer requests repair work that will exceed $350, to prepare a written repair estimate before performing any diagnostic work or repair, unless the customer waives the estimate in writing. The $350 figure includes parts, labor, diagnostic and teardown charges, taxes, shop supplies and incidental services. The estimate must include a statement letting the customer indicate whether replaced parts should be saved for inspection or return, and the daily storage charge after the repair is complete. Shops must post a sign at least 24 inches on each side stating these rights. A customer injured by a violation may sue for damages, costs and attorney's fees.
local_facts.why_it_matters: A mobile mechanic is a motor vehicle repair business under the same article. The written quote before work, and the old parts back on request, are rights a Wilmington driver already has; this site expects them on every job, threshold or not.

local_facts.title: New Hanover's emissions test is on its way out; the safety inspection stays
local_facts.claim: On May 11, 2026 the EPA proposed approving North Carolina's request to remove its vehicle inspection and maintenance program, the emissions test, from the State Implementation Plan for the remaining 19 counties, with only Mecklenburg County continuing emissions testing under state law. New Hanover County is among the counties named. NC DEQ had proposed ending the test in 18 counties including New Hanover in August 2024. The annual safety inspection remains a condition of registration renewal statewide.
local_facts.why_it_matters: Once the change takes effect a check-engine light alone no longer fails a Wilmington inspection, but brakes, lights, tires and wipers still do, and a mobile mechanic can fix those before the station visit. Only a licensed station can issue the sticker.

local_facts.title: A thousand-year flood put cars under water in September 2024
local_facts.claim: In September 2024 a stalled coastal storm dropped more than 18 inches of rain on Carolina Beach in 12 hours and almost 21 inches overall, described as a 1,000-year rainfall event. A state of emergency was declared in New Hanover, Brunswick, Bladen and Columbus counties; homes flooded, cars were submerged, schools closed, and roads including U.S. 17 in Brunswick County and U.S. 74/76 were shut. Saltwater immersion corrodes brake lines, fuel lines, subframe components and suspension hardware at a rate cleaning does not reverse, and a flooded car can start and drive normally for months before an airbag module, transmission controller or ABS sensor fails.
local_facts.why_it_matters: Flooded cars from that storm and from earlier hurricane seasons are in the local used-car supply. The under-carpet, under-seat and connector checks in a pre-purchase inspection exist for this reason.

local_facts.title: Coastal heat takes seventeen months off a battery
local_facts.claim: AAA, citing Consumer Reports data, states that vehicle batteries in the southern United States on average last 17 months less than in colder northern climates, because heat accelerates grid corrosion inside the battery, and that under-hood temperatures can exceed 150 degrees in some regions.
local_facts.why_it_matters: Wilmington adds salt air to the heat, which corrodes terminals and ground straps. A battery past three years old here is a candidate, and a load test is the honest way to tell a dead battery from a corroded connection.
